t: Make Individual Performance Transparent to the Team
q: This transparency creates the unique optics of peer pressure that go unspoken but have a tremendous influence on individual results.
Too many leaders are reluctant to create transparency for fear they will embarrass low performers and demotivate anyone not performing at the top.
Going from no transparency to full transparency is indeed a recipe for reactive disaster.
In a metric-open workplace, team members can’t hide from the data.
Truth be known, the pressure to perform is created almost entirely by the desire to meet the expectations of peers, not leaders.

t: How To Handle A Bossy Colleague
q: We’ve all been annoyed by the bossy colleague who is constantly giving advice and pushing you to do things their way.
It’s to calmly and respectfully repeat the same phrase whenever they begin pressuring you to do (or teach) anything you don’t want to do.
Now, if they follow up by asking why not, just say “It’s a good idea, but not right for me.” There is no need to go on and on or explain further.
You have to stand up for yourself in this profession to avoid the kind of stress that will cause you to quit teaching.
Speaking up can feel awkward and the last thing you want to do. But the discomfort is only for a few minutes then gone forever.
They’ll begin to view you as a strong, independent, and competent teacher who doesn’t need their constant input.

t: When It Comes to a Critical Choice, Ask an Equally Critical Question
q: This critical decision influences treatment and has a profound impact on whether a patient survives or not.
By answering any of these three critical questions in the affirmative, any doctor can reach a quality decision regarding immediate and high risk.
Consequential choice decisions that are repetitive in nature can normally be boiled down into one or more critical questions that streamline the decision.
Here’s an all-too-common episode that unfortunately plays out every day somewhere.
A patient suspecting a heart attack is rushed to a hospital for emergency care.
The attending physician must quickly decide whether the sufferer should be treated as a high-risk or low-risk patient.
Yet, there are so many factors to consider, many of which have to do with a patient’s history.
Too often, the patient is either inaccurate about these factors or is not able to communicate clearly.

t: Unpacking a Student Letter
q: All that I would like to do in today's article is unpack how the note describes changes in Finn's Five Key Beliefs.
It's easy as an adult to forget that this stress is experienced as pain. It's not fun. And, according to Yerkes-Dodson, while some stress is good for enhancing human performance, too much is NOT.

Boring" and "dumb" are from the lexicon of anti-Value. When our students bring this to us, we can meet this kind of language objectively, even gratefully. They are showing us what they believe, giving us insight into their hearts.

One of the most delightful ways to become more Credible as a teacher is to train your soul to enjoy the work of teaching. But I'm very serious with that word "train." The soul must be trained to like the students, the content, and the challenging task of connecting the two.
Humans want to fit; we want our social context to align with our identity. But then — height of heights — she began to feel that she belonged. She felt like she was "supposed" to be there.
It is, indeed, one of the greatest feelings around. And this, colleague, is why you and I can be so confident in the value of what we offer — we offer one of the greatest feelings around.
It took several months for Finn to get used to the idea of not taking results personally and unpacking outcomes.

t: Observe Average Teachers, Too
q: If you are inspired by a good book, there's always the danger of plagiarism, of doing something that is too much like that good book. Whereas, a genuinely helpful reaction to a piece of work that you're reading is, '[My goodness], I could write this [stuff]!'
To me, Moore's advice is super apropos to teachers. Just as Moore advises writers to read terrible books, so, too, should teachers observe average teachers.
The LAST THING that you want in this job is to become arrogant or self-righteous. These states warp the soul. They make you less.
The job, when rightly approached, has a built-in humbling feature. I'm not talking about demeaning yourself when I say "humbling;" I'm talking about taking yourself less seriously.
But sometimes, when you keep struggling day after day with that ONE student or that ONE class period, you can start to think, "Gosh, I'm UNIQUELY lousy at this.

And when you go, do it with honor for the person. Yes, you are going to privately notice in the observation some areas that are not as great as the things you do. But look, too, for areas of strength.
What I hope you take from observing average teachers — what I have taken away, many times — is greater clarity, greater confidence, and greater inspiration for the work tomorrow holds.

t: Developing an Ethic of Accountability
q: For leaders with this ethic, whatever happens always starts with them.
They accept and own any outcome, asking what they did to contribute to it, or what they could still do to change it.
A leader with a strong accountability ethic immediately points to themselves and presumes they have some role in the reticence the team displays.
Some people always look to external factors for whatever goes wrong and point to themselves only when things go right.
They present themselves differently, ask questions others don’t ask, and balance short and long-term goals masterfully.
Perhaps most distinctive about them is the view they have about responsibility.
Over the course of their lives, they have created an ethic of accountability for themselves.
They immediately take responsibility, not the blame, for whatever outcome, reaction, or result that occurs.

t: How Many Roberts Do You Know
q: Who you know really matters, and as your network grows, so does the probability of good fortune.
There are roughly 4.3 million Americans named Robert, which is just over 1% of the population.
If you know 10 Roberts well enough to have their contact information and to have had a conversation with them in the past two years, then you likely have a personal network of 1,000 people.
Nothing produces opportunities like an ever-expanding network.
As personal networks expand during a career, so do learning opportunities, job offers, invitations to attend life-shaping events, and occasions to be a part of special experiences.
So, estimating the size of your personal network and those of your team members can be an illuminating exercise.

For those teams and team members dependent on an expanding network to achieve goals, such as sales and fund-raising teams, assessing how many people an individual knows and connects with is often a predictor of success.
Unfortunately, accurate estimates of personal networks are difficult to come by.

t: Lubricating the Mind and Body Before Performance
q: Before every show, Miller does a 30-minute vocal warm-up while walking on a steeply-inclined treadmill.
The minute I open my mouth, I want to sing any song as good as you ever heard it.
Without a consistent warmup routine to lubricate the mind and body and to boost self-confidence, even talented and highly polished professionals will find it hard to be at their best every time.
The essential power of warming up is well-known and religiously applied by high performers in nearly every endeavor.
Even intellectual tasks benefit from physical warmup routines, such as stretching and a brisk walk to get the blood flowing and to increase the oxygen supply to the brain.
Top performers believe in lubricating the mind and body before they perform.
Some turn to reading, solving brain puzzles, or drawing as ways to prime the mind and get it ready to perform.
Almost everyone rehearses some of the same actions the performance requires, sometimes in slow-motion or faster motion to get the cobwebs out or to focus on deliberate actions.

t: Taking Charge Is Not About Getting Your Way
q: Those who must take charge falsely believe that without them things won’t happen.
Taking charge when the situation calls for it is very different from the need to get your own way.
Leaders who have a deep-seated need to control situations and take charge are uncomfortable not directing action.
So how does a leader with a bias for action know whether they are actually leading or simply controlling by nature? The answer lies in how they follow.
Great leaders are also great followers. They don’t always need to be in charge or direct the action.

t: On experience and reflection in teaching
q: Mr K wants to improve his practice and asks to observe a more experienced teacher, Ms Y.
It could be due to Ms Y’s experience. The mistake I used to make is to equate experience with time spent teaching. But experience is way more than that: it is reflection in disguise.

This teacher might reflect on this and think using mini-whiteboards is not worth the effort and time it is taking to build a routine of whole class participation and thinking. But if the purpose of using the mini-whiteboards (increasing ratio) is not achieved via another, possibly more effective strategy in this context, then the self-reflection is flawed.
Reading something in a book and then observing it in action is incredibly useful CPD. However, in Mr K’s case, it wasn’t enough.
Simply knowing about the importance of techniques such as Checking for Understanding is not enough to help teachers improve their practice.

I have been Ms Y (possibly not as successful as her!) where a trainee once asked me similar questions and I replied with ‘I just knew what to do’. Entirely unhelpful, I know, but it did make me go away and think about how I responded to the class and the decisions I made.

t: A Nice Worksheet
q: Worksheets are just pieces of paper with math problems on them. The specific problems and the way they fit together can be good or bad.

If I'm giving students problems on whiteboards I'm progressive or I value student-centered learning or the whole child or something. If I'm giving students problems on paper I'm a boring old traditionalist. That's silly.
The worksheet led to some great conversations about how percents are commutative — 30% of 50 is the same as 50% of 30, etc.
Students had been kindof grudgingly working on the double number lines with a lot of prodding from me as I ran around. Suddenly they were focused and grinding on the worksheet.
Worksheets become a problem when there's too much repetition and students stop thinking, or when they're the only pedagogical tool a teacher uses.
A worksheet can be a pleasant change of pace when students are mentally tired.

t: 3-Read Friday #19: Reflection, Worksheets, and Christmas Maths
q: This is a powerful post about the challenges novice teachers face when observing their more experienced colleagues.
The best part is that Jo gives us a series of questions that teachers of all experiences can ask when they watch their colleagues in action in order to understand the reasons behind their decisions.

He describes why he chose to use a particular worksheet in the vain of the intelligent practice activities on my variation theory website, and contrasts this with two more challenging questions he asked his students later in the lesson.
The point about a worksheet making students (and possibly teachers) feel safe really resonated.

Colleen has done a great job of compiling the very best Christmas-themed maths resources and advent calenders out there to ensure you can inject some festive fun into your lessons whilst also keeping your students thinking hard about maths.

t: Learning to Think on Your Feet
q: Speed in response requires being prepared with answers or responses to almost any question or challenge.
The best comedians work painstakingly hard at thinking through every reaction, response, and trajectory of a joke.
Knowing a wide variety of topics extremely well makes leaders faster on their feet more often.
What looks like magic is really just hard work and repetition.
The mental agility to quickly process information and to respond instantaneously is a highly prized skill.
When put on the spot or asked an unanticipated question, the ability to think on your feet and respond in real-time with a clever or pointed answer suggests a powerful mind.
Leaders who exhibit this skill in any conversation are thought to be smart and quick-witted, dazzling in their replies without a second’s delay.
Like a magic trick we observe but can’t figure out, we want to know how they do it.

t: The Tyranny of the Vocal But Minor Voice
q: When team members feel fully comfortable expressing their opinions and views, they naturally do so, often loudly and insistently.
Leaders who lack the courage to confront extreme advocacy and behavior inadvertently allow a vocal and minor voice to hold the team captive.
When any view sounds like a crusade, it needs to be negated.
Good leaders work hard to create the conditions where everyone on the team feels comfortable and safe offering their candid views.
Allowing a space for all voices, views, and concerns helps to create a more inclusive workplace.
The openness of a team that feels supported in expressing opinions not only improves morale, but also leads to higher-quality decisions.
As worthy as the goal of an inclusive and open team dynamic might be, however, it also has a downside.
Good leaders listen, consider what has been said, and thank team members for their contributions.

t: Dear Workaholic Colleague
q: Human beings can only take so much pressure before their performance declines. Psychologists Yerkes and Dodson codified this idea over 100 years ago with what I call the Yerkes-Dodson Curve.
When you add the stakes to the dehumanizing nature of so many of our policies and systems, it's a mundane observation to say that over-pressure is the default.

A major cause of teacher attrition, by my observation, is when we as teachers allow our jobs to become our source of identity. If you can't look in the mirror and see more than a teacher, more than a person with all these job responsibilities and all these student problems to handle, you're on the path to burnout.

When an identity-enmeshed teacher fails, their whole soul writhes in agony. The bad day in the classroom becomes so much more than just that; it becomes an indictment of our human value, a spiritual judgment that we are lacking and inadequate as a human being.

On the other hand, when an identity-enmeshed teacher succeeds — when they win an award, when their students outperform the average on tests, when they get compliments in the grocery store from students or their parents — it is as if they've taken a hit of a spiritual cocaine.
In both cases, the end result is losing your sense of self, losing the kind of rootedness that is required for a flourishing life.
Thankfully, the best medicine for such dilemmas is often as simple as rest.

t: What Bill Watterson Teaches Teachers
q: Your classroom is an alternate world from the one your students normally inhabit. Or at least, it should be. It's a cosmos—Latinized from the Greek kosmos: a good order, an orderly arrangement; a world.
But when you read Calvin and Hobbes, a related truth emerges: our kids are a cosmos, too.
It turns out Calvin's a lot more than a first grade mischief-maker. He's a cosmos. What his teacher sees is only a sliver of who he is.
In rereading Watterson's strip, I find in myself a growing capacity for relishing a bit of the mischief some of my students bring to class, too.
Watterson was not just insightful — he was an artist, and he lavished his excellence at a level uncalled for by his medium.

Watterson was something rare in today's world: a human being in touch with their finitude. He had only so much time, so much energy. He wanted to keep these precious resources focused on where he could do his greatest good — on his comic strip.

It's always better to leave when you're not sure that you should than to stay around until everyone's sure that you should." In the interview Burke expanded on this, saying, "I wanted to leave while I still loved it.

My interests have shifted however, and I believe I've done what I can do within the constraints of daily deadlines and small panels. I am eager to work at a more thoughtful pace, with fewer artistic compromises.

t: Organizing Meetings Around Questions Instead of Topics
q: A simple way to promote more discussion and to get people excited and ready to contribute is to cast each topic or issue as a question.
The best agenda questions pose a challenge, presume an end state, or suggest a root cause.
Meetings, agendas, and topics organized by questions create a more vibrant dialogue between team members.
That’s because any point that is not an answer to the question becomes obvious and can be brushed aside as irrelevant.
Effective meetings are driven by agendas and often include a variety of issues, topics, and discussion points.
Naturally, leaders organize meetings topic-by-topic to keep the discussions focused and on track.
Look at virtually any meeting agenda at nearly any enterprise, and you will find a topic or issue-driven agenda.
While there is nothing wrong or problematic with this well-worn approach, it has one Achilles heel: it doesn’t promote dialogue or intense debate unless the topic is highly charged for team members.

t: People Who Project Their Own Flaws Onto Others
q: People with deep insecurities have a peculiar habit. They commonly project those insecurities onto others.
By attributing their own flaws to others, they avoid having to examine and deal with those deficiencies.
When a leader or colleague has an exceptionally strong reaction to something you say or do that has no basis or reasonable explanation, they are likely projecting their insecurities onto you.
In other words, whatever flaw they struggle with is often the focus of their behavior with others.
For instance, leaders who ridicule others about their lack of confidence often struggle with their own self-confidence.
Similarly, colleagues who struggle with holding themselves accountable often blame others for their lack of responsibility.
Any time a person shifts the focus from their own shortcomings onto others, they are said to be projecting .
While everyone projects now and again, people (especially leaders) with deep insecurities do so frequently, creating misinformation disguised as feedback.

t: In Search of More Gamma Brainwaves
q: The electrical activity emanating from the brain is displayed in the form of brainwaves, ranging from high activity to low activity.
At the Gamma state, we achieve our most optimal mental and physical performance.
Music with binaural beats creates an auditory illusion when two slightly different frequencies are presented separately.
Brainwaves have a big impact on the body and mind, influencing mood, sleep, focus, energy, and physical coordination, among many other functions.
For instance, Theta waves are present during times of deep relaxation, whereas Delta waves occur when we are sleeping or drowsy.
Beta waves reflect active thinking and sustained focus, while Alpha waves are present when we are learning and engaging creatively.
In the Gamma state, our self-awareness reaches its most acute level, giving us a heightened sense of creativity and insight.
In this mental frame, we are most likely to find a state of “flow.” When in flow, distractions disappear, as we become so immersed in the task at hand that we lose track of time.

t: Where Do Leadership Instincts Come From
q: In our estimation, they seem to know things we wouldn’t expect them to know.
Decisions steeped in values can never be fully wrong, and the best leaders know that; therefore, they apply them religiously to every judgment and decision they encounter.
When leaders combine deep, past experience with core values, something magical happens. They operate from what looks like instinct.
We often refer to highly effective leaders, especially those with less experience or background, as having great leadership instincts.
More importantly, these people land on a good or right answer seemingly without much effort.
They are instinctively good at leadership, or so we believe.
Technically speaking, an instinct is an intuitive way of assessing and acting on a situation or problem.
Instincts are thought to be baked into the biology, family history, and personality of those who possess them.

t: What Is Conceptual Understanding Good For?
q: What is the point of conceptual understanding? I often find myself teaching something in the name of conceptual understanding but without a very clear goal of what I want students to learn.
Humans forget things. If students only have a procedural understanding of something, when the procedure gets hazy they are prone to make silly mistakes.
Standard algorithms are great in lots of situations, but they are also inefficient in others. Conceptual understanding can offer students an alternate path in certain situations.
Students want to feel like math makes sense and to know why a rule works or why a procedure is what it is.
New knowledge sticks best when it's connected to prior learning. Conceptual understanding is the stuff that connects concepts and creates those links.
I want to have clear goals when I try to teach conceptual understanding to ensure students are learning something useful and not foundering with fuzzy knowledge.

t: The coachee continuum: how coachable are you?
q: Live coaching is one way we make our time ‘alive time’ – stepping in, in the moment, in order to slightly improve our craft, perfectly captures the idea of actively using time usefully.
It occurred to me though, we haven’t given a lot of attention to how we RECEIVE live coaching.
The response examples on the continuum clearly indicate that the live coaching has not been successful. Neither of the two criteria have been fulfilled.
As much as it is the coach's responsibility to fulfil the criteria of effective feedback, so too is it the coachee's.
Your ego screams for people to acknowledge you. But you must do nothing. Take it. Eat it until you’re sick. Endure it.
Be coachable. Make your time ‘alive time’. Be on the right side of the coachee continuum.

t: Skills vs knowledge, 13 years on
q: The problem is we did not make sufficiently clear that skills are the accumulation of knowledge. Without knowledge there can be no skills.

When you dig into the research, you find that the best way to teach these complex skills is by breaking them down into smaller parts, teaching those smaller parts, and gradually combining together the constituent parts in increasing complexity.
Data from the last 40 years lead to a conclusion that is not scientifically challengeable: thinking well requires knowing facts, and that's true not simply because you need something to think about.
Asking what the right balance is between knowledge and skills is like asking what the right balance is between ingredients and cake.

Every time a teacher tried to fill in the gaps and teach a lesson focussing on times tables, or historical chronology, or the meaning of new words, inspectors and advisers would tell them that this was not in keeping with the curriculum.
The Sunday Times quotes Keir Bloomer as saying that these statements are 'childish rubbish.'

t: 3-Read Friday #18: Skills vs Knowledge, Live Coaching, and Conceptual Understanding
q: It’s the post that everyone has been reading this week, but I wanted to flag it up just in case you have missed it.
Daisy revisits the skills versus knowledge debate with the clarity and nuance that only she can, reflecting on the troubles that Scotland’s skill-based Curriculum for Excellence has encountered.
It was Thahmina who first introduced me to the concept of live coaching.
In this fantastic post, Thahmina digs deeper into the concept of live coaching, addressing one of the potential barriers: the ego of the person being coached!

Dylan does a far better job than I ever could of providing a framework to help us think about the role conceptual understanding plays in learning, and some concrete strategies to help our students acquire it.

t: The Familiarity Trap
q: When he's going over the problems in class it makes so much sense. But then when I go to do it myself, I can't figure it out. This is called the "illusion of competence" — or, in my parlance, the Familiarity Trap.
The mind — yours, mine, our students' — is designed for avoiding needlessly hard work. This is why familiarity — "I watched the teacher do it and it made sense" — is such a problem.
But all that these common study practices do is reinforce familiarity. The students don't know the material any better after doing these common studious actions. They're just more familiar with it.
The key is creating more situations where students are actually required to call up and apply the information they are learning.
What you want is to create what researcher Robert A. Bjork calls "desirable difficulty." This is when the learner struggles to retrieve learned information and use it on their own.
Too much difficulty, and the learner will shut down. Too little, and they'll remain in the Familiarity Trap.

t: Testing for Grit
q: The idea of grit refers to a person’s ability to persevere and remain determined in the face of challenge, adversity, or obstacles.
Those with grit bounce back from setbacks, displaying a resilience to cope with whatever is thrown at them.
In behavioral interviews, leaders can learn when candidates have walked away from a challenge and why.
Some leaders and organizations prefer to use puzzles or case studies to test for grit.
The quality of grit, or a passionate persistence, is considered a priceless attribute when hiring prospective team members.
People with grit maintain a commitment to long-term goals and consistently work toward them despite the difficulties that may arise along the way.
They don’t allow obstacles to become a distraction or to derail them from achieving their goals.
Gritty team members share a host of positive assets, including a growth mindset and the ability to maintain a deeper focus on long-term goals.

t: How To Handle Students Who Need Your Attention
q: They follow you around and pull on your hem. They ask a zillion questions and expect your personalized attention.
Students who crave attention mean well. They’re not trying to annoy you or get under your skin. The truth is, their behavior is learned.
They get their way by never taking no for an answer. They’ve discovered that the squeaky-wheel strategy works.
If needy students are unable call out and unable get up from their seats without raising their hand and asking permission, then you limit their ability to reach you.
Force them to rely on their own wits until they realize it’s futile to ask you and that they can indeed trust their own judgment.
Behavior, confidence, and academic ability will all improve. Most of all, however, is maturity, which will skyrocket. They’ll become different people in a few weeks.

t: The Hidden Jeopardy of Expected Rewards
q: In fact, any time a leader or organization repeats a reward two times or more, it becomes an expected or calculated reward.
The only time an expected reward really matters over time is when it doesn’t happen. Then, it is remembered forever.
Expected rewards that don’t occur carry a deep symbolic meaning to people.
The key is to remember not to repeat a reward, no matter its popularity, twice in a row.
Expected or calculated rewards are the enemy of great leadership. The idea is not to create them in the first place.

t: Feedback is Fire (But LOTS of Teachers Misunderstand and Overcomplicate It) ercomplicate-it
q: It's gotta be quick — if I've forgotten what I was thinking when I did the thing I'm getting feedback on, I'll be unlikely to use the feedback. It's gotta be intelligible — if it doesn't make sense to me, I'll be unable to use it.
When even one of these traits is absent, the helpfulness of feedback dwindles rapidly.
By far the most effective method of feedback I employ as a teacher, then, is in-the-moment feedback on what students are working on.

As my students discuss unit review questions in pairs, I walk around, listen in, and give verbal feedback to help them hone their answers, illustrate concepts with concrete details, or clarify vague thinking.
This kind of feedback is so effective, in fact, that I've long done away with grading pop-up debates with a rubric.
The in-the-moment feedback is so much more powerful than the next day rubric because it's 1) timely, 2) intelligible, and 3) manageable.
For both of these applications of the science of learning, they need to know how the practice is going and what to make of their test results. For both of these, they'll need feedback.

t: A Salute Returning a Salute
q: A Confederate general riding near the front of the procession appreciated the gesture from Chamberlain and ordered the same posture to be returned by his troops.
The idea of the losing team showing respect for the victors has become deeply ingrained into the ideals of good sportsmanship.
We confer a rare and exalted character to leaders who go out of their way to show respect to those on the losing side.
The best leaders know that the ultimate right to be respected is won by respecting others, especially the vanquished.
In a ceremony at the conclusion of the Civil War, just outside of Appomattox, Virginia, the Confederate Army of the South laid down their weapons before the Union soldiers of the North.
Grant asked 4,000 soldiers to line up at attention on one side of the ceremonial battlefield.
Lee’s defeated infantry units were to march onto the field and place their regimental flags and weapons at the foot of the Union officer in charge.

As the Confederate contingent entered the field, the commanding Union officer, Joshua Chamberlain of Gettysburg fame, told the Union soldiers to “carry arms,” a posture of respect whereby soldiers hold the rifle in their right hand with the muzzle perpendicular to their shoulders.

t: Designating an Angels Advocate
q: Hearing all of the viewpoints, positive and negative, allows the team to make the best decision possible.
Leaders understand the power of the Devil’s Advocate , someone who plays the role of chief doubter and critic in the discussion of an important decision.
The Advocate plays an important role by pointing out the downside, potential risks, and likely problems associated with a decision or strategy.
Leaders sometimes designate a team member to play this role, although there is usually one colleague who does so without being asked.

Given that leaders and teams often get behind an idea, decision, or strategy with a big momentum forward, and without questioning the downside, it seems unlikely that someone who points out the upside and opportunity at hand would add much value.
Just like a Devil’s Advocate is not just a critic or skeptic, an Angel’s Advocate doesn’t just focus on the positive or cheer the team on.
Instead, an Angel’s Advocate asks the “What If?” question and points out the possibilities if the decision and strategy were successful.
Such an Advocate focuses most on what would change as a result of a successful outcome, highlighting the many benefits that are hard to visualize during the decision process.

t: The First 10 Minutes
q: This first part of each lesson is crucial in setting your expectations, routines, grabbing students’ attention and setting the tone for the rest of the lesson.
I start practically every one of my lessons in the same way, so that students feel safe in knowing what to expect when they enter my room and so that it becomes habitual.
These are retrieval questions on prior learning, not just the last lesson in case students were absent.

I haven’t outlined my procedure above in the hopes that all teachers will copy everything I do in those first 10 minutes but rather to show how I have carefully thought about and made explicit everything that I want to happen in that time.
Script and practice saying want you want students to do, making your explanations clear and concise.

t: Execution over resources: Two ways to use the same slide.
q: Recently I ran a whole school CPD session about the concept of checking for listening (CfL) as a way of helping students pay attention to key areas.
When we consider the think ratio the two options significantly diverge. In 1 the think ratio is low. The teacher is asking the question at the end and all the information is on the slide.
Cognitive load theory suggests that the fact that reading written words and listening to speech are processed through similar channels of the working memory.
This accountability or ‘threat of inference’ helps motivate them to pay attention.
Resource design is important, but it’s not the only important thing. It’s easy to focus on because it has an artifact that we can evaluate at the end.

t: Are You a Should or Could Leader
q: Using the word Should is not a request. It is an imperative demand, even if offered politely or with the intention of helping others.
When it comes to feedback, Could represents a sharing of power and changes the command to a suggestion to consider another option.
Directing people to do things differently invariably means dropping the Should bomb.
It is an imperative demand, even if offered politely or with the intention of helping others.
When leaders use the word Should , they do so from a place of power, expertise, or experience.
As such, they direct people to a different action or choice.
We empower others to make the call when we replace Should with C ould .

You should add another story to the presentation” has a very different implication than the statement, “You could add another story to the presentation.” The former statement is a directive, and may even be interpreted as a mandate or command.

t: 3-Read Friday #17: Teaching Klaxons, Checking for Listening, and the First 10 Minutes
q: I love this list of things teachers should try to avoid saying or doing… all of which I have said and done many times, of course.
There are few surer ways to prevent a student from admitting they are struggling than by labelling a question in that way.

Adam does an amazing job in this blog comparing two ways of checking students are listening to an explanation that appear really similar on the surface, but one of which is likely to cause students to pay significantly more attention.
Jody outlines exactly what the first 10 minutes of their lesson looks like, and the rationale for each step.
What happens at the start of the lesson sets the tone for what follows.

t: 10 Classic Klaxons… Things to avoid doing or saying
q: I often imagine that classrooms could be wired with a QI studio wall klaxon that flashes and sounds an alarm when contestants say the obvious but wrong answer.

These checks are invariably met by a murmur or some nodding heads. Nobody says anything. Zero information is exchanged but the teacher takes it as a cue to proceed – often with undesirable consequences.
It's just not enough. The value of asking a follow-up question is huge especially when each answer has to take account of the previous one.
Hanging her out to dry just reinforces everyone’s sense that being unsure is a terrible thing to reveal. It’s a total own goal.
One example contains two sets of information: the general rule or pattern you want students to learn AND the specifics of that specific example. You can’t see a pattern from one thing.
If they don’t practice and consolidate- there’s not going to be much learning.

t: Test Stress and Anxiety are Not Inevitable
q: It's unpleasant and painful for students. When it becomes too much, it diminishes student performance (as all over-stressed situations do, per the Yerkes-Dodson Curve).
This self-identification as a bad test-taker produces anti-Belonging, which starts to trigger what I call an Anti-Belonging Doom Loop.

I asked my students to raise their hand if they feel at least 1% stressed or anxious during a test. My purpose here was to help normalize struggle, and sure enough, about 80% of hands went up in each class.
The good news, though, is that performance-inhibiting test stress and anxiety are solvable problems, provided that we give students the right kind of practice prior to tests.

Folks in Group B performed better than folks in Group A in both conditions. (This makes sense based on what we know about retrieval practice; it's such an important concept that I cover it at length in another of the principles — "Tests are the Best" — in my upcoming course.) But here's the cool part: folks in Group B saw no performance decline in Condition 2, whereas folks in Group A did significantly worse in the stressed condition.
In short: using retrieval practice as a study method not only improved test performance in general, it erased the performance declines you and I often see when test stress/anxiety are present.
What's the application? Teach your students retrieval practice! Use it in your class. Incorporate retrieval practice as often as you can.

t: How To Handle Unplanned Interruptions
q: Events and incidents out of your control invade your well-ordered peace like the hordes of Cimbri.
Your present mood and disposition also transfer to your students. The more anxious and frustrated you feel, the worse they’ll behave.
Well, here at SCM we’ve long promoted the benefits of maintaining a professional distance—from students, from the job, and from situations out of your control.
But it takes work. It takes daily practice. It takes discipline to work at it every day until it becomes second nature.
For those who practice the discipline of never getting too invested or deep in the emotive weeds, unexpected events act as a trigger to draw back, run cooler, and breathe deeper.
Yes, the unexpected will still strike at the worst possible time. But it will no longer ruin the moment, let alone your whole day. A penny on the tracks, nothing more.

t: How Leaders Overestimate and Underestimate Their Own Brain Power
q: Leaders commonly overestimate their own thinking and brain power in areas where they lack expertise and underestimate their cognitive abilities on topics where they are highly competent.
Technically known as the Dunning-Kruger effect, this bias raises concerns about when leaders should trust their own instincts and abilities and when they shouldn’t.
In essence, some leaders weigh what others think way too much when they themselves are the true expert in the room.
Because it is invisible to those affected by it, this bias can severely skew an important decision.
Having a more objective view regarding your true expertise and skill is the most important step in combatting this pervasive bias.
The first principle is that you must not fool yourself and you are the easiest person to fool.

t: Upward Feedback or Complaint
q: By expressing their dissatisfaction through complaint, team members are asking the leader to own their problem or issue and to resolve it.
Leaders prefer to engage with team members who have a ready-made solution for the problem they have identified or experienced.
The distinction between a complaint and feedback is often missed by many team members because of their need for catharsis.
Make it a rule never to offer a criticism upward without a solution or suggestion to go along with it.
Talented team members don’t complain. They refuse to act as victims.
They remember that upward feedback always amplifies the solution, not the problem or the dissatisfaction.

t: When a Colleagues Ideas Are Repeatedly Ignored
q: Not every idea a colleague proposes is a good one. But when a pattern emerges where many or most of the ideas a team member suggests are ignored or overlooked, there is a good reason left unexplained.
Most notably, the reputation and credibility of the colleague makes their ideas suspect. In other words, others don't view them as competent or savvy.
When proposers lack conviction, confidence, or clarity, it is difficult for others to get behind and elevate an idea.
In many organizations, hierarchy determines who is worthy of offering a new idea and when. Without the status to be heard, the idea will simply be passed over or discarded.
Having your ideas rejected on a regular basis is hugely disconfirming and undermines the confidence to speak up at all.

t: The Most Important Technology in My Classroom
q: There's no question about the most useful technological marvel that my students and I use to grow in mastery of my discipline: the spiral notebook. These little 70-page beauties can be had for $1.50 at our local grocery store.
They require no charging. I've never had a student complain of a log-in issue. No one forgets their password. They've yet to be disrupted by ChatGPT.

If it seems like I'm being a little silly, there is a little bit of that going on here. But a big part of that silliness comes from the joy I have at knowing that these simple tools form the logistical backbone of the work of learning I facilitate in my room each day.

But that learning isn't powerful just because it's happening in spiral notebooks. It's powerful because it's informed by 10 key principles of learning that I've taken away from cognitive science over the years.
And yet, they absolutely undergird each decision I make in my classroom — including my decision to lean so heavily on high-tech solutions like spiral notebooks.
I don't lead in-person workshops on these topics. I don't have any books on them. I've written about them here and there on the blog, but never in an organized or deep manner.

t: Do You Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think
q: People can think through the issue by reading, listening, and contemplating where they stand on the topic and then speak, OR they can talk out loud and clarify their views through their own words and through the dialogue they create with others.

In team meetings, those who Think-to-Talk can appear overly calculated and unwilling to fluidly explore ideas, whereas those who Talk-to-Think can come across as unpolished and unprepared to articulate a view.
In contrast, those who prefer to learn what they think as they talk need interaction to gain clarity and conviction about what they believe.
Because they know others can become impatient with their need to speak to learn, they often warn others that they are “thinking aloud here.
They recognize that differences in how team members go about thinking and speaking are a strength, not a weakness.

t: Creating Bookend Routines
q: Losing control over their own tasks and priorities can be both unsettling and frustrating. Good leaders must learn to cope with this reality.
Taking charge of the day is always possible at the bookends, the beginning and ending of the day.
So, consider establishing a routine for the first 30 minutes after rising for the day. Execute this routine before checking news and email and responding to others.
Repeating the same routine every morning tells your brain you’re ready to tackle the day with vigor and with a positive frame of mind.
Creating bookend routines gives leaders the opportunity to maintain complete control over the most important parts of the day.

t: Team Celebration Is the Glue That Binds People Together
q: Of the many forms of praise, including compliment, recognition, and approval, none is as energizing or motivational as celebration.
Celebration tells others to sit up and take notice of what has been achieved.

It is not the event or trappings of the celebration, nor the positive experience that creates its impact. Celebration is symbolic. It brings people together in a collaborative spirit of connectedness.
The fear that celebrated team members will slack off or presume success before the work is complete is unfounded.
The best leaders quickly learn that the more they celebrate, the more accomplishments there are to honor. Funny how that works.

t: The Right Leader for the Challenge
q: In his esteemed view, the military leader who excels in peacetime is not necessarily the leader who excels in wartime.
More typically, leaders with a particular skillset perform best when the challenges they face call for their exact skills.
Disappointing a highly talented leader is never painless, but making the wrong call based on loyalty isn’t what the organization needs most.

Because relationships, loyalty, and payback for hard work and past success color so many promotion decisions, selecting the best leader for the current challenge is exceedingly hard for organizations.
Selecting the leader with the skills and talents to confront the challenge we face is among the most important decisions any organization will make.

t: QLAs – How to Use Them Well
q: Question level analysis (big old spreadsheets which look very colourful and contain data about how every student did on every question) are time consuming to produce and, by themselves, are not useful.
When you see a big column of red under a question title, do not just assume everything about that topic needs to be retaught.
It is your job when reviewing whole class assessments to do the greatest good for the greatest number, teaching those things well is better than teaching everything poorly.
This data is going to be produced as a result of the teaching this class had. As well as being reactive in the moment to this class don’t forget to be proactive as well.
You need to diagnose the gap in their understanding and teach more holistically. That exact question won’t come up again, make sure you fix the cause, and not just the symptom.
I think QLAs can be an incredibly powerful tool but it’s important to remember that is all they are, a tool.

t: Product of Primes: Extending and Deepening Understanding nderstanding/
q: In moving schools, there’s often also a move in curriculum. Mostly, this affects the sequencing of content, and as such, the links you emphasise while teaching.
In this task, the first column uses variation to explore how changing the number alters it’s product of primes.
I’ve kept the power of 17 throughout the entire task to strong-arm pupils into considering the structural relationships with their powers rather than writing everything out in expanded forms.
When teaching this, I’ve found students lack the flexibility to think about commutativity when it forms part of the ‘why’ something works.
I think a lot of this comes down to the ‘finding an answer’ mindset that can override pupils’ willingness to play with structure.

t: Improving teaching: getting over the knowing-doing hump -knowing-doing-hump/
q: I never use one. I do have one, but haven’t touched it for about 2 years.
This isn’t a post about visualisers though. It’s about why getting teachers to change anything about their practice is really hard.
Peps Mccrae summarises this nicely in this thread, and suggests one of three problems that lead to this gap, and some potential solutions
Perhaps it might be better to think of the distance between knowing and doing as a hump rather than a gap.

For a novice teacher, perhaps a visualiser would represent something of a quantum leap, allowing them to do a whole host of things they weren't doing before. But for more experienced teachers it may be that there is only a marginal gain to be had.
The insight provided by a coach may result in sufficient motivation to nudge us over that hump.

t: 3-Read Friday #16: the Knowing-Doing Hump, QLAs, and Product of Primes
q: This fascinating post from Paul looks at the reasons teachers may not make changes to their practice, even though they know it is the right thing to do.
Paul illustrates the issues through his own desire to use a visulaiser more, which has never materialised into actually using a visualiser more.
I chose this one because I have long had an issue with Question Level Analyses (QLAs): they take ages to fill out, and I am not convinced they have a positive impact on student learning.
Craig is more positive than me, discussing seven ways teachers can use QLAs more effectively.
Dan does exactly this for the product of prime factors, discussing the sequencing of the lessons, together with the quality resources he has assembled.

t: Why Some Teachers Continue To Struggle With Classroom Management agement/
q: So what follows are five reasons why some teachers continue to struggle year after year with classroom management.
You see, they’re not meant to be used together. Each SCM strategy, for example, is made to mesh with and make every other SCM strategy stronger and more effective.
To be successful, you have to be well-versed. You have to know why the strategies work and how best to use them, which takes study and reflection.
Rest assured, the conditions you’re experiencing, no matter how bad they seem, are the same as thousands of other teachers right now.
Deep down they don’t want a peaceful classroom because then there won’t be anything to rail against. So they sabotage themselves.
You have to throw away the deceptions and doubts, embrace the burden and responsibility, and decide: “I can do this and nothing will stop me.

t: Two Simple Questions to Help Students Improve Performance in Your Current Unit ent-unit
q: Is it possible to help your students significantly deepen their understanding of your current unit, regardless of content area? Yes. And it need only take 5-10 minutes of class time.
First, identify a handful of concepts that are especially important for the unit your students are working on.
As the students wrestle with your questions, walk around. Look at what they are doing on the page. Ask them about where they are struggling. Do let them struggle a bit.
When you ask students to think about the relationships between key concepts in your course, you're asking them to do what cognitive scientists call elaboration.

Going back as far as 1975, researchers have been demonstrating that when students think about the meaning of what they are tasked with learning, their ability to retain and use what they've learned increases.

Ultimately, we want to teach our students how to do this kind of elaboration themselves. This is what researchers did in another study where learners were taught elaboration techniques and then performed better on subsequent tests of memory.
Whether the course interests you are not, try asking your students to compare 2-3 key concepts tomorrow. Let me know how it goes.

t: The Skills Required Before Accountability
q: Often overlooked, however, are two essential skills that enable team members to become accountable in the first place: the ability to keep commitments to colleagues, and the dedication to follow up on everyday tasks and activities.
It is much more common for colleagues to become distracted and forgetful about the small commitments they have made to others.
In too many instances, they are left high and dry by a colleague who has not completed a task they are depending on to finish their work.
Leaders who demonstrate this skill through their example help others see the importance of follow-up, but it is not enough.
Laying the skillful foundations for accountability is essential work. Effective leadership is often created brick by brick.

t: Energizing the Team That Faces Repetitive Tasks and Travel
q: Leaders and team members who are repetitively tasked with the same assignments, travel, and engagements often lose energy and enthusiasm for the work over time.

Players have a tendency to go sideways on you, not for any other reason than fatigue, boredom, monotony. Eighty-two games, 30 cities, same place, same arenas, same locker rooms, same hotels, same food.
Great leaders don’t accept the idea that monotony and fatigue are inevitable and must simply be endured.
Doing the same task or assignment is only monotonous if it is done with the same approach, with the same thinking, and with the same people.
The cure for boredom is curiosity and great leaders encourage it, sometimes to the point of insisting on it.
